content: In biology, the term precocial refers to species in which the young are relatively mature and mobile immediately after birth or hatching. In contrast, the term altricial describes species whose young are born in a helpless state. Some species that exhibit an extreme form of precocial development are referred to as superprecocial. These categories—precocial, altricial, and superprecocial—exist along a continuum without clear boundaries between them. Precocial species are typically nidifugous, meaning they leave the nest shortly after birth. This developmental strategy is particularly diverse in birds. Precocial birds, such as many ground-nesting species, hatch with well-ossified skeletons, functional vision, and feather coverage. However, many precocial chicks are not immediately capable of thermoregulation, meaning they cannot regulate their own body temperatures. They rely on their parents to provide warmth through brooding for a short period. Precocial birds are capable of finding their own food, although they may receive assistance or instruction from their parents. Examples of precocial birds include domestic chickens, various species of ducks and geese, as well as rails and crakes. The most extreme example of precociality is seen in megapodes, whose chicks dig themselves out of the nest mound without any parental assistance and are capable of flight on the first day after hatching. Precociality is not limited to birds; it is also observed in other animal groups. Familiar examples of precocial mammals include most ungulates, guinea pigs, and many species of hares. Interestingly, this trait is not evolutionarily conserved, as closely related species can exhibit different developmental strategies. For instance, hares are precocial, while rabbits are highly altricial. Precocial species generally have longer gestation or incubation periods compared to their altricial counterparts. They also tend to produce smaller litters or clutches, as each offspring must reach a relatively advanced and larger developmental stage before birth or hatching. The phenomenon of imprinting, famously studied by Konrad Lorenz, is characteristic of precocial birds. The term precocial is derived from the same root as precocious, both of which imply early maturity. From a phylogenetic perspective, precociality is thought to be the ancestral condition in birds. Altricial birds, on the other hand, are more commonly found in the most evolutionarily derived groups. There is evidence suggesting that precociality was present in some protobirds and troodontids, as indicated by studies conducted by Elzanowski (1995) and Varricchio et al. (2002).
